units.text: We'll patch a fleet without treating patch policy and timing as the same choice. The baseline defines approved patches, while the maintenance window schedules an operation. A compliance scan identifies missing approved updates; installation actually attempts to apply them.

Start with a small group and verify service health before another wave. Plan for reboot and capacity. These are operational safeguards you design; a patch task succeeding does not by itself prove the application stayed healthy.

State Manager can associate a reviewed configuration with nodes selected by tags and run it on a schedule. In this example, one agent configuration differs. The next successful run can bring it back and report compliance.
Check targeting, last run and the relevant agent signal. That is different from running a one-time command. If a node cannot communicate, the association won't instantly repair it.

An alarm detects a symptom. With the configured integration, it can create an OpsItem that records the affected work, priority and owner. Inspect related evidence rather than assuming every alert has already been correlated.
The operator decides how to respond and verifies the result. An OpsItem tracks that work; it doesn't automatically fix the application just because the alarm created it.

We'll decide whether a worker fleet should scale even though C P U looks low. Queue age and backlog reveal work accumulating faster than the workers can finish it. Choose a demand signal that matches the service objective.

In this example workers increase from four to twelve and queue pressure falls. Check downstream capacity before scaling further and validate the time needed for new workers. A lower C P U percentage alone doesn't prove the queue recovered.

When a target fails a health check, the load balancer handles traffic to the targets it considers healthy. An Auto Scaling group can replace the instance based on its configured health checks. Tie the behaviors together deliberately; they are not one operation.

Keep persistent application state outside the instance when the design requires it. Configure warmup and draining appropriately. Verify the replacement is ready and serving before counting it as recovered capacity.

We'll diagnose missing logs at the first boundary that fails. Check that the application wrote the file and that the agent reads the intended path. Here the agent reports AccessDenied, which tells us to check delivery permission rather than opening an inbound port.
Check the instance role's actual permission for the intended log destination. Correct only the missing access. Generate a harmless test record and verify the expected text and timestamp arrived.

For this subscription, keep the log group and logical destination in the same Region. Check whether the destination policy permits the source account, and whether the delivery role may write to the intended stream. Verify each boundary independently.

Send a harmless test event and check the destination stream. A published subscription filter doesn't prove records reach their target, and a differently located backing stream can be supported even though the logical destination is regional.

Checkout errors rise just after a deploy. That's a good lead, but rule out other causes with logs and traces. Downstream alerts may reflect the same failing request; group them for investigation without ignoring their evidence.

If evidence supports rollback, use the approved procedure and verify checkout and its dependencies recover. Don't assume duplicate alerts disappear automatically just because the primary metric improves.

We'll patch in controlled waves. Drain an initial target, run the approved patch operation, and verify the application after it returns. Then choose wave sizes that preserve healthy capacity across the locations you depend on.

If the health check fails, pause future waves. Error thresholds can stop new dispatch while in-flight operations finish. Use the agreed rollback or replacement path rather than assuming a patched machine is automatically ready.

A worker tier can fall behind because a message keeps failing or because there isn't enough healthy capacity. Use queue and worker evidence to tell them apart. A dead-letter queue isolates repeated failures; it doesn't create more workers.

Replace or restore unhealthy capacity as appropriate, then verify age, failures and customer-facing recovery improve. Ensure workers handle repeat delivery safely so backlog recovery doesn't apply the same order twice.
